title: The Design of Everyday Things
author: Don Norman
target_audience: Design professionals (UI, UX, product, industrial designers)
Students and educators in design or cognitive sciences
General readers interested in how things work
core_themes: Cognitive psychology principles in everyday objects
Iterative design and the importance of testing
primary_purpose: To illustrate the importance of intuitive, user-centered design in everyday objects by analyzing common design flaws, explaining how well-designed things function, and providing principles for making products easier to use.

structure_format.organization: Seven chapters divided into focused topics including the psychology of everyday actions, principles of good design, and practical solutions for common design issues
features: Case studies illustrating both poor and successful design

key_concepts_lessons: Design should prioritize usability and user experience above aesthetics.
Affordances and signifiers clarify how objects are to be used.
Feedback helps users understand the results of their actions.
Constraints prevent user error and make misuse less likely.
Human error is often a consequence of poor design, not user stupidity.
Iterative prototyping and user testing are essential for creating better products.
Understanding how people think and behave is crucial for effective design.
notable_features: Numerous relatable examples drawn from daily life
Widely used as a foundational textbook in design education
cultural_historical_context: Initially published in the late 1980s when personal computing, electronic devices, and complex gadgets were becoming prevalent, the book highlighted user frustration and the need for design grounded in human cognition. Its renewed edition reflects a further evolution toward digital interfaces and smart technologies.
reception_impact: Seminal work in the design and usability fields; considered required reading for designers and engineers
Introduced key terminology into both academic and practitioner vocabulary (‘user-centered design’, ‘Norman doors’)
Influenced generations of designers and product developers
Praised for making design accessible and fostering empathy for users
comparable_titles: Don't Make Me Think by Steve Krug
The Inmates Are Running the Asylum by Alan Cooper
About Face by Alan Cooper, Robert Reimann, David Cronin, Christopher Noessel
